1352.title: Life cycle close
1352.hook: a life, from the adhan in the ear to the prayer without an adhan
1352.howItsDone: Some Muslim families say the adhan softly in a newborn's ear, and at the end of life the community washes, shrouds and prays over the body in a funeral prayer that has no adhan; on hearing of a death, the words of Qur'an 2:156 are said: "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning."

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance: the shares the Qur'an names, with something and a kind word for those present. Today, the whole road at once.

A baby, a few hours old, in someone's arms. A parent or a grandparent leans in close to the tiny right ear and says the adhan, softly: Allahu akbar. Some families do this, and it's where this stretch of the path began. Now the other end of the road: a funeral. People stand in rows behind the imam for the funeral prayer, and before it, no adhan is called at all. Some people put those two moments side by side and say a life is the space between the call and the prayer. That's a saying people tell, not a verse. But it makes a good map.
screen: `THE CALL IN A NEWBORN'S EAR.` → `A PRAYER WITH NO CALL.` → `A LIFE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: Walk the road again, and watch whose hands do the work. At the start, someone else says the call in your ear, touches a softened date to your mouth, chooses your name, shares the meat of the sacrifice, shaves your hair and gives its weight in silver. You're carried. Then the middle, and the hands become yours. Learning to pray. Finishing the Qur'an, the khatm. Coming of age, when the duties begin. Choosing a spouse, giving consent, the nikah, a home where, as surah al-Rum puts it, two people may dwell in tranquility. Serving a family, shepherding a flock, honoring the elders who once carried you. Then the road bends: visiting the sick, remembering death. And at the end, the hands go back to the community. Someone washes you, wraps you in plain white cloth, stands in rows to pray over you, lays you facing the qiblah, cooks for your family, writes the shares of what you left. The Qur'an says it plainly in surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's words: "Every soul will taste of death." And surah al-Baqarah describes the patient, who say when misfortune strikes: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." So the shape of a Muslim life, as these customs draw it, is carried, then carrying, then carried again. The middle is the part a person lives with their own hands, and that's where the path goes next: the festival year.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR CALL.` · `THE MIDDLE IS YOURS TO LIVE.` · `SOMEONE ELSE SAYS YOUR PRAYER.` · `CARRIED, CARRYING, CARRIED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Ask, without hurrying: where am I on the road right now, being carried, carrying someone, or somewhere in between? Notice who carried you to get here, and who you're carrying now, even in a small way, without judging the stage. If you pray, you can remember the people at both ends of your road.
Life cycle close. The whole road, from the adhan in a newborn's ear to the funeral prayer that has no adhan, with the community's hands at both ends. Today's word.
Your line: from call to prayer. The middle is yours to live. Tomorrow, the sacred months.

1353.title: The sacred months
1353.hook: four sacred months: Muharram, Rajab, Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah (9:36)
1353.howItsDone: The Islamic calendar treats Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab as sacred months, named in a hadith of the farewell sermon in al-Bukhari; Qur'an 9:36 asks people not to wrong themselves in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the life cycle closed: carried, then carrying, then carried again. Today, a new stretch: the year itself.

The verse begins by counting. Surah al-Tawbah, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months by Allah's ordinance in the day that He created the heavens and the earth." A calendar, built into creation. Then it marks some off from the others: "Four of them are sacred." It doesn't name them. For the names, you go to a sermon the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave at the farewell pilgrimage. Which four, and what makes a month sacred?
screen: `TWELVE MONTHS WITH ALLAH.` → `FOUR OF THEM ARE SACRED.` → `WHICH FOUR?`

segments.voice: You met some of these months one by one back in year two. Today, the frame that holds them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Bakrah reports the Prophet's words at the farewell pilgrimage, in paraphrase: the year is twelve months, and four of them are sacred. Three come one after another: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah and Muharram. The fourth stands alone: Rajab, the one between Jumada and Sha'ban. Three in a row, and one on its own. Back in al-Tawbah, right after "Four of them are sacred," the verse says: "So wrong not yourselves in them." Notice who gets protected. Not the month. You. Some commentators read it as saying wrongdoing weighs heavier in these months, the way a careless word lands harder in a holy place. So sacred time works like sacred space. A mosque is still a building, with walls and a floor, but you walk in differently. These four months are still ordinary weeks, with work and errands and laundry. The calendar says: walk in differently. Slower to quarrel. Quicker to do good. And because the months are named and fixed, nobody has to decide each year when to be more careful. The calendar decides. Over the coming days, the path walks through the year: Muharram, the other months Muslims keep, all the way to Ramadan and the Eids.
screen: `THREE IN A ROW, AND RAJAB ALONE.` · `SO WRONG NOT YOURSELVES IN THEM.` · `SACRED TIME, LIKE SACRED SPACE.` · `THE CALENDAR DECIDES FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: On each slow breath, say one name: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram, then pause for the gap in the calendar, and say Rajab. Go round again, three and a pause and one, until the shape feels familiar. Then think of one place where you already walk in differently, a room, a grave, a kitchen table, and let the four months feel like that place.
The sacred months. Four of the twelve, named in the farewell sermon: Dhul Qa'dah, Dhul Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab on its own. Times not to wrong yourselves. Today's word.
Your line: four sacred months. Three in a row, and one on its own. Until tomorrow.

1354.title: Muharram: the month of Allah
1354.hook: the best fasting after Ramadan is in Muharram (Muslim)
1354.howItsDone: Some Muslims keep voluntary fasts during Muharram, following a hadith in Sahih Muslim that calls it Allah's month and praises fasting in it as the best after Ramadan; the fast is voluntary, not required.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sacred months: three in a row, Rajab alone, and a verse that says, wrong not yourselves in them. Today, one of the four, up close.

After Ramadan, which fast is best? In Sahih Muslim, that question is put to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and Abu Hurayrah reports his answer. It doesn't name a single day. It names a whole month, and gives that month a title you won't find printed on a calendar page. Not the month of the new year. Not the month of fasting. The month of Allah.
screen: `AFTER RAMADAN, WHICH FAST?` → `A WHOLE MONTH.` → `THE MONTH OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here is the hadith, in paraphrase: the best fasting after Ramadan is in Allah's month, al-Muharram, and the best prayer after the obligatory prayers is the prayer at night. One sentence, two offerings: an empty stomach by day, a person standing awake at night. Then the name. Every month belongs to Allah, Muslims say, so why call this one Allah's month? Some scholars explain it the way they explain the phrase house of Allah for a mosque. Every place is His, but naming one place after Him lifts it and sets it apart. And Muharram is already one of the four sacred months, the third of the three in a row. You met it back in year two as the start of the Islamic year, as tradition counts it. Now the part that's easy to miss: none of this is required. Ramadan's fast is a duty. Muharram's is an offer. The word in the hadith is best, not must. Nobody is told to fast the whole month. A person can take one day, or a few, and they're stepping into what the hadith praises. So Muharram is an open door at the start of the year. And it gives the fast a life outside Ramadan. A practice that only happens once a year can start to feel like a costume. A voluntary day in Muharram says the fast belongs to ordinary time too.
screen: `A FAST BY DAY, A PRAYER BY NIGHT.` · `WHY CALL IT ALLAH'S MONTH?` · `AN OFFER, NOT A DUTY.` · `THE FAST IN ORDINARY TIME.`

segments.voice: If you fast, pick one day this Muharram, or the next time it comes, and see it on the calendar in your mind; if you don't, choose something small to hold back from for one day, a snack, a scroll, a second coffee. Notice what it's like to choose an offering nobody requires of you. If you pray, you can remember the night prayer the same hadith praises.
Muharram. A sacred month, called Allah's month in Sahih Muslim, where voluntary fasting is praised as the best after Ramadan. Today's word.

1355.title: Ashura: two ways
1355.hook: a Sunni fast and a Shia commemoration, each explained by its own people
1355.howItsDone: Sunni practice includes a voluntary fast on Ashura, sometimes with the day before it, following hadiths in al-Bukhari and Muslim; Shia Muslims keep Ashura as a day of mourning for Husayn ibn 'Ali at Karbala, with gatherings called majalis, recited elegies, processions in some places, and the giving of water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muharram, Allah's month, with its fast praised as best after Ramadan. Today, one day inside it.

Same date, two rooms. In one kitchen, before dawn, a family eats quietly so they can fast through the day, thankful for a rescue in the time of Musa. Across town, people dressed in black fill a hall in the evening. Someone recites, slowly, the story of a grandson of the Prophet and the thirst of his family, and people weep. At the door, volunteers hand out cups of water. Both are keeping Ashura.
screen: `A FAMILY FASTING BEFORE DAWN.` → `A HALL IN BLACK, A STORY RECITED.` → `THE SAME DAY.`

segments.voice: You met both ways back in year two; today, side by side. First, the fast, as Sunni Muslims explain it. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a report from Ibn 'Abbas. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Madinah, he found the Jews there fasting on the day of Ashura. He asked why. They told him, in paraphrase: it's a good day, the day Allah saved the Children of Israel from their enemy, so Musa fasted it. He answered: I have more right to Musa than you. So he fasted it, and told people to fast. In Sahih Muslim he says he hopes the fast of Ashura wipes away the sins of the year before, and in another report, that if he lives to the next year, he'll fast the ninth as well. So some Sunni families fast the day before too. Second, the commemoration, as Shia Muslims explain it. On Ashura, the histories say, Husayn ibn 'Ali, the Prophet's grandson, was killed at Karbala with members of his family and companions, after days cut off from water. For Shia Muslims, the day is one of mourning. They gather in majalis, where the story is told and elegies are recited. In some places there are processions. Water is given out, in memory of the thirst at Karbala. Shia speakers describe Husayn's stand as a refusal to bow to injustice, and grief for him as keeping faith with that stand. Third, these aren't strangers to each other's day. Sunni tradition honors Husayn too: a hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls Hasan and Husayn the leaders of the youth of Paradise. One date, two ways of keeping it, and each makes sense from inside.
screen: `A FAST FOR MUSA'S RESCUE.` · `A MOURNING FOR HUSAYN AT KARBALA.` · `SUNNIS HONOR HUSAYN TOO.` · `ONE DATE, TWO WAYS.`

Then shape one curious, gentle question you might someday ask a neighbor about how their family keeps Ashura. If you pray, you can remember Musa's rescue and Husayn's family together.

1356.title: Rabi' al-Awwal
1356.hook: the month of the Prophet's birth and death, marked differently by different Muslims
1356.howItsDone: Some Muslims mark the Prophet's birth in Rabi' al-Awwal with a mawlid gathering of Qur'an recitation, poetry in his praise, stories of his life and shared food; others, following scholars who hold it shouldn't be set apart as a festival, keep the month like any other and honor him by following his example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashura: a Sunni fast for Musa's rescue, a Shia day of mourning for Husayn. Today, another month kept more than one way.

Someone asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about fasting on Mondays. A practical question. His answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, isn't practical at all. In paraphrase: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came down to me. So he marked the day of his own birth, every week, with a fast. Some Muslims recall that answer when a particular month comes round each year: Rabi' al-Awwal, the month tradition gives for his birth, and for his death.
screen: `WHY FAST ON MONDAYS?` → `THE DAY I WAS BORN.` → `A MONTH REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an never gives the date of his birth. The early biographies place it in Rabi' al-Awwal, and tradition places his death in the same month. Al-Bukhari keeps a report that he died on a Monday, the day of the week he was born. The exact day of the month is remembered differently by different communities. Then the celebration, as those who keep it explain it. Some Muslims mark his birth with a gathering called the mawlid, which you met back in year two. People recite the Qur'an, sing poems in his praise, tell the story of his life and share food. They describe it as joy at a mercy, and point to surah al-Anbiya, in Pickthall's words: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples." If Allah sent a mercy, they say, it's right to be glad of it, and they point to the Monday fast as his own way of marking the day. Then the restraint, as those who hold back explain it. Other Muslims, and some scholars, hold that his birth shouldn't be set apart as a festival, because the Prophet and his companions didn't do so. They keep the month like any other, and say their love for him is no less. For them, the way to honor him is to follow his example every day, and they point to surah al-Ahzab: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example." Notice what both share. Nobody is arguing about whether to love him. They differ about how to show it. Both say they're doing it for him.
screen: `A BIRTH AND A DEATH IN ONE MONTH.` · `THE MAWLID: JOY AT A MERCY.` · `HOLDING BACK: FOLLOW HIM DAILY.` · `BOTH SAY: FOR HIM.`

1357.title: Rajab and Sha'ban
1357.hook: the months of preparation before Ramadan
1357.howItsDone: Some Muslims add voluntary fasts in Sha'ban, following 'A'ishah's report in al-Bukhari that the Prophet fasted most in that month outside Ramadan, and make up missed Ramadan fasts before the next one begins; some communities also keep the night of the middle of Sha'ban with extra prayer, while others don't set it apart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabi' al-Awwal: a mawlid for some, an ordinary month for others, and love for him on both sides. Today, the two months before the big one.

'A'ishah lived close enough to notice his habits, including the shape of his fasting through the year. In Sahih al-Bukhari she says, in paraphrase: I never saw him fast a complete month except Ramadan, and I never saw him fast more in any month than in Sha'ban. So the month right before Ramadan wasn't a pause, a last chance to eat before the fast. It was the month he fasted most of all, outside Ramadan itself.
screen: `WHAT 'A'ISHAH NOTICED.` → `MOST OF ALL IN SHA'BAN.` → `THE ROAD UP TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, Rajab. You met it a few days ago, the sacred month that stands alone between Jumada and Sha'ban, and back in year two as well. So the run-up to Ramadan begins inside sacred time, with the verse still ringing: wrong not yourselves in them. Second, Sha'ban, and why. In a report kept by al-Nasa'i, Usamah ibn Zayd asks the Prophet: I don't see you fast in any month the way you fast in Sha'ban. His answer, in paraphrase: it's a month people neglect, between Rajab and Ramadan, and a month in which deeds are lifted up to the Lord of the worlds, and I love for my deeds to be lifted up while I'm fasting. Squeezed between a sacred month and the month of the fast, it's easy to skip. He didn't. Third, catching up. 'A'ishah says in al-Bukhari that when she owed fasts from the last Ramadan, she would make them up in Sha'ban. So it's also the month for settling accounts. Fourth, the middle of Sha'ban. Some communities keep that night with extra prayer, remembering the dead and asking forgiveness. Other scholars hold that the reports about that night are weak, and they don't set it apart. Both sides speak from the reports as they read them. Put together, it's a runner's warmup. Nobody wakes up and races. Rajab and Sha'ban are the stretching: a little fasting, a little extra prayer, old debts cleared, so when Ramadan opens, the habits are already moving.
screen: `RAJAB: SACRED TIME FIRST.` · `SHA'BAN: THE MONTH PEOPLE NEGLECT.` · `CATCHING UP ON OLD FASTS.` · `A WARMUP, NOT A PAUSE.`

segments.voice: Whether or not you'll fast in Ramadan, pick one small habit you'd like to be steady by then: waking a little earlier, reading a page a day, a few minutes of quiet. Picture doing it tomorrow, at the exact time and place, and the day after; a warmup is small on purpose. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it.
Rajab and Sha'ban. The two months before Ramadan: a sacred month, then the month the Prophet fasted most outside Ramadan, a time people neglect. Today's word.
Your line: getting ready. A warmup, not a pause. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

1358.title: Ramadan: planning
1358.hook: a plan for reading, prayer, charity and rest
1358.howItsDone: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan, and some make a plan beforehand for reading the Qur'an, night prayer, charity and zakat, and enough sleep and food at the pre-dawn meal, drawing on Qur'an 2:185 and hadiths in al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rajab and Sha'ban: sacred time first, then the month he fasted most outside Ramadan. Today, the door opens.

A sheet of paper taped to a fridge door, a few days before the new moon. Four words across the top: reading, prayer, charity, rest. A portion of the Qur'an a day. Which nights at the mosque. Who gets the zakat, and when. What time the alarm goes off for the meal before dawn, and what time the phone goes off at night. It doesn't look holy. It looks like a schedule. But some families do exactly this before Ramadan, because a month can slip past on good intentions alone.
screen: `A SHEET OF PAPER, FOUR WORDS.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE A SCHEDULE.` → `A MONTH CAN SLIP PAST.`

segments.voice: You met Ramadan on day six, and walked through its days in year one. Now, how to arrive on purpose. Begin with reading, because the Qur'an ties the month to the book. Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion." Ibn 'Abbas reports in al-Bukhari that Jibril would meet the Prophet, peace be upon him, every night of Ramadan and go over the Qur'an with him. So a reading plan follows the habit Ibn 'Abbas describes. Then charity, which the same report ties to the reading: the Prophet was the most generous of people, and most generous of all in Ramadan when Jibril met him, more generous, he says, than a wind sent out. Then prayer: in another hadith in al-Bukhari, whoever stands in prayer through Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward is forgiven past sins. Then rest, the column people forget. The same verse says: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." The month is meant to be hard enough to change you, not so hard it breaks you. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells people to eat the meal before dawn, because there's blessing in it. Sleep, food and water are part of the plan, not a failure of it. And look back at this week: the life cycle closed, then the year opened, the sacred months, Muharram, Ashura, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rajab and Sha'ban, all walking toward this one month.
screen: `READING: THE MONTH OF THE BOOK.` · `GIVING, LIKE A WIND SENT OUT.` · `REST: ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.` · `A WEEK WALKING TOWARD ONE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Picture the sheet of paper and its four words, and give each one a short line: a realistic amount of reading a day, one time of prayer you'll protect, one person or cause to give to, one thing you'll keep for rest. Keep each line short enough to actually do. If you won't fast, the same four words still work for any month you want to keep well.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, the month al-Baqarah says the Qur'an was revealed in, with room for reading, prayer, charity and rest. Today's word.
Your line: plan the month. A plan is how you arrive on purpose. Tomorrow, the family table.
